title: Visual Cycle — DOMiNANCE Originals
source: KNUST Visual Cycle lecture (Edwin F. Laing) and accompanying study guide

questions.stem: Which retinal photoreceptors primarily support vision in dim light?
questions.why: Rods respond to much weaker illumination than cones because their responses integrate light signals over time and rod pathways pool input. They therefore support scotopic vision.

notes.A: Cones chiefly support colour and fine spatial detail at higher light levels.
notes.B: Bipolar cells relay signals from photoreceptors to downstream retinal neurons rather than capturing light for scotopic vision.
notes.D: Ganglion cells are the retinal output neurons. Ordinary scotopic image formation begins with rods.
notes.E: Horizontal cells integrate signals laterally between retinal pathways rather than serving as the primary dim-light receptors.

questions.stem: Which photoreceptors chiefly permit discrimination of colours in bright light?
questions.why: Cone classes contain opsins with different spectral sensitivities. Comparing their responses distinguishes wavelengths under photopic illumination.

notes.A: Rods contain a single rod visual pigment and cannot by themselves distinguish colours.
notes.B: Amacrine cells modify signalling in inner retinal circuits rather than supplying the three light-sensitive inputs to colour vision.
notes.C: Ganglion cells encode and carry cone-derived signals, but they are downstream of the photoreceptors used for colour discrimination.
notes.D: Bipolar cells relay photoreceptor responses, including cone responses, to downstream retinal cells.

questions.stem: Early night blindness with loss of peripheral vision suggests preferential injury to which cells?
questions.why: Rods predominate outside the central fovea and support the high sensitivity needed at night. Preferential peripheral rod degeneration can explain both night blindness and constricting visual fields.

notes.A: Foveal cones chiefly support central acuity and colour, so preferential loss would affect central rather than early night vision.
notes.C: Bipolar cells transmit input from both rods and cones, making their nonspecific injury less characteristic of this combination.
notes.D: Ganglion-cell axon damage can affect visual fields, but selective early night blindness points more specifically to the rod pathway.
notes.E: Iris muscles control pupil size and do not encode peripheral visual fields.

questions.stem: Which dietary substance serves as a plant-derived precursor of vitamin A?
questions.why: Beta-carotene is a provitamin A carotenoid. Cleavage can yield retinal, which can be reduced to retinol or used to make other vitamin A derivatives.

notes.A: Arachidonic acid is a polyunsaturated fatty acid and eicosanoid precursor rather than a provitamin A carotenoid.
notes.B: Cholesteryl esters store or transport cholesterol and do not furnish the retinal carbon skeleton.
notes.C: Palmitoylcarnitine participates in mitochondrial transport of long-chain fatty acyl groups.
notes.E: Phosphatidylserine is a membrane phospholipid rather than a source of provitamin A activity.

questions.stem: Which dietary source supplies mainly preformed vitamin A rather than provitamin A carotenoids?
questions.why: Fish liver oil supplies preformed vitamin A, chiefly as retinyl esters. Plant sources generally provide carotenoids that require conversion to active retinoids.

notes.B: Yellow vegetables may contain carotenoids that can be converted to vitamin A.
notes.C: Orange sweet potato is rich in beta-carotene, a precursor rather than preformed retinol.
notes.D: A plant carotene extract contains carotenoids that may have provitamin A activity.
notes.E: Green leafy vegetables can provide beta-carotene, even when chlorophyll masks the carotenoid colour.

questions.stem: What chemical group distinguishes retinal from retinol?
questions.why: Retinal has a terminal aldehyde, whereas the corresponding group of retinol is a primary alcohol. Oxidation of the alcohol gives the aldehyde.

notes.A: Neither of these vitamin A derivatives is defined by a phosphate substituent.
notes.B: Further oxidation of retinal gives retinoic acid, which contains a carboxyl group.
notes.D: A sulphate group is not part of the defining structure of retinal.
notes.E: The difference is the oxidation state of the terminal carbon, without addition of a sugar.

questions.stem: Why can the 11-cis-retinal chromophore respond strongly to visible photons?
questions.why: Retinal has alternating single and double bonds that allow electrons to delocalise. This conjugated system absorbs light, and photon absorption can drive isomerisation about a double bond.

notes.A: The retinal chromophore contains no phosphorylated amino group.
notes.B: Retinal is a conjugated organic aldehyde and has no covalent phosphate chain.
notes.C: Light absorption arises from the chromophore's electronic structure and does not require a mitochondrial enzyme.
notes.D: Cation channels respond downstream to changes in cGMP and are not part of the light-absorbing chromophore.

questions.stem: Which molecular transformation initiates the light response of rhodopsin?
questions.why: Photon absorption changes rhodopsin-bound 11-cis-retinal into the all-trans configuration. The resulting change in chromophore shape drives activation of opsin.

notes.A: Regeneration of 11-cis-retinal from all-trans retinoids occurs in the visual cycle after light capture.
notes.C: Retinoic acid is a vitamin A derivative involved in signalling, while rhodopsin activation uses retinal isomerisation.
notes.D: Activation involves a change in retinal geometry without addition of a phosphate group.
notes.E: Carotene can supply vitamin A precursors, but conversion of dietary carotenoids is separate from the immediate light response.

questions.stem: Which component supplies rhodopsin with its light-absorbing chromophore?
questions.why: The light-absorbing portion of dark-adapted rhodopsin is 11-cis-retinal. It binds covalently to opsin and changes configuration on photon absorption.

notes.A: Rhodopsin kinase phosphorylates activated pigment in signal shut-off and provides no chromophore.
notes.B: Guanylate cyclase makes cGMP, a signalling nucleotide downstream of light capture.
notes.C: Arrestin helps terminate signalling by binding activated, phosphorylated rhodopsin.
notes.E: Transducin alpha relays the signal from activated rhodopsin rather than absorbing the photon.

questions.stem: Which linkage attaches the retinal aldehyde to an opsin lysine residue?
questions.why: The retinal aldehyde condenses with the epsilon-amino group of a lysine to form a protonated Schiff base.

notes.B: Disulfide bonds join two cysteine sulphur atoms, neither of which is the linking group in this pigment.
notes.C: An ester forms from an alcohol and an acid derivative, whereas retinal reacts here through an aldehyde.
notes.D: Peptide bonds are amide bonds linking amino acids in proteins.
notes.E: The covalent bond uses retinal's aldehyde and the lysine amino group without a phosphate bridge.

questions.stem: What explains the difference in light absorption between free retinal and intact rhodopsin?
questions.why: The protein binding pocket and Schiff-base protonation shift the chromophore absorption spectrum.

notes.A: Spectral tuning does not require a phosphatase because no phosphate bond needs to be hydrolysed.
notes.B: Cytochrome c normally transfers electrons in mitochondria and is unrelated to the pigment's absorption shift.
notes.D: Transducin is a signal-relaying G protein and does not glycosylate retinal.
notes.E: Rhodopsin kinase phosphorylates activated rhodopsin rather than cleaving the chromophore to tune its spectrum.

questions.stem: Which approximate wavelength is the absorption maximum of intact rhodopsin?
questions.why: Intact human rod rhodopsin has an absorbance maximum near 500 nm because the opsin environment tunes its bound retinal. This is a pigment measurement rather than the peak of overall scotopic visual sensitivity.

notes.A: The near-ultraviolet value is well below the measured absorbance maximum of human rod pigment.
notes.B: The wavelength is blue and shorter than the blue-green absorbance peak of intact rhodopsin.
notes.C: The wavelength lies in the red part of the spectrum, far above the rod pigment peak.
notes.D: The value lies in the blue range, short of the typical rhodopsin maximum of about 500 nm.

questions.stem: Why does vitamin A deficiency commonly cause early night blindness?
questions.why: Vitamin A supplies the retinal chromophore needed to regenerate rhodopsin after light exposure. With less pigment available, rods fail first in their role of detecting very dim light.

notes.A: Photopsins are cone visual pigments, and excess photopsin is not the mechanism of night blindness in vitamin A deficiency.
notes.C: The relevant shortage is an outer-segment chromophore rather than a change in vitreous hydration.
notes.D: Altered glucose use does not explain the lack of vitamin A-derived substrate for pigment renewal.
notes.E: Retinal pigment epithelium melanin absorbs stray light but is distinct from the retinal chromophore in rhodopsin.

questions.stem: Which photolytic rhodopsin intermediate can activate transducin?
questions.why: Metarhodopsin II is the signalling state reached after light-driven retinal isomerisation. It activates transducin by promoting GDP release from its alpha subunit.

notes.A: Metarhodopsin I is a precursor in the photointermediate sequence and is not the principal transducin-activating state.
notes.B: Bathorhodopsin is an early intermediate that forms before the signalling conformation.
notes.C: Lumirhodopsin is an earlier photointermediate on the pathway towards metarhodopsin II.
notes.E: Free retinal lacks the activated opsin conformation required to interact productively with transducin.

questions.stem: Why is a rod membrane relatively depolarised in the dark?
questions.why: In darkness, cGMP binds cyclic nucleotide-gated channels in the rod outer segment. Inward sodium and calcium current keeps the membrane relatively depolarised despite continued potassium efflux.

notes.B: PDE hydrolyses cGMP, tending to close the cation channels rather than maintaining their dark-state opening.
notes.C: Arrestin normally acts on phosphorylated rhodopsin during shut-off and does not block potassium channels.
notes.D: Retinal is a chromophore and does not transport sodium across the outer-segment membrane.
notes.E: Transducin regulates phosphodiesterase after illumination, while a separate exchanger handles calcium extrusion.

questions.stem: How does illumination typically change the membrane potential of a rod photoreceptor?

options.label: B
options.text: It initiates a sodium action potential

questions.why: Light activates phosphodiesterase through rhodopsin and transducin, lowering cGMP and closing outer-segment cation channels. The drop in inward current makes the membrane potential more negative.

notes.A: Depolarisation is characteristic of the dark current. Illumination reduces that current.
notes.B: Rods signal with graded changes in voltage rather than firing sodium action potentials in response to light.
notes.D: Potassium efflux continues during the reduction of inward cation current and helps drive hyperpolarisation.
notes.E: The initial rod response is a graded hyperpolarisation rather than a depolarising plateau.

questions.stem: After rhodopsin activation, what happens to guanine nucleotide bound to transducin alpha?
questions.why: Activated rhodopsin promotes release of GDP from transducin alpha. GTP from the cytosol binds the vacated site, activating the G protein.

notes.A: ATP and AMP are adenine nucleotides rather than the guanine ligands of transducin alpha.
notes.B: The bound GDP first dissociates. Activation does not require adding phosphate to that molecule.
notes.C: Cyclic AMP is a second messenger, whereas the activating ligand of transducin alpha is GTP.
notes.D: cGMP is hydrolysed downstream by PDE and is not the nucleotide exchanged on transducin.

questions.stem: Which enzyme is activated by GTP-bound transducin alpha?
questions.why: Transducin alpha bound to GTP activates the photoreceptor phosphodiesterase PDE6. PDE6 hydrolyses cGMP and decreases the opening of cyclic nucleotide-gated channels.

notes.A: Retinal guanylate cyclase restores cGMP during recovery rather than mediating its light-driven breakdown.
notes.C: Adenylate kinase interconverts adenine nucleotides and is not the effector of transducin.
notes.D: Rhodopsin kinase helps terminate pigment activity by phosphorylating the activated receptor.
notes.E: The enzymes of retinal isomerisation help renew pigment and do not mediate the immediate transducin response.

questions.stem: What event directly closes cyclic nucleotide-gated channels following a flash of light?
questions.why: The outer-segment channels remain open when enough cGMP is bound. Light activates PDE6, so unbinding as cGMP concentration falls directly promotes closure.

notes.A: An increase in cGMP favours channel opening, as occurs during response recovery.
notes.B: The channel's gating ligand is intracellular cGMP, so extracellular ATP depletion does not directly close it.
notes.C: Retinol participates in the visual cycle but does not set the gating state of these channels.
notes.E: Chloride concentration is not the direct gating signal for the cGMP-sensitive cation channels.

questions.stem: How does light generally alter glutamate release from rod synapses?
questions.why: Light hyperpolarises the rod and reduces opening of voltage-gated calcium channels at its synaptic terminal. Less calcium enters, so exocytosis of glutamate falls.

notes.B: Increased glutamate release is typical of the relatively depolarised dark state.
notes.C: The response changes vesicle release rapidly without requiring glutamate synthesis to cease.
notes.D: Acetylcholine is a distinct neurotransmitter and is not formed from rod glutamate on illumination.
notes.E: Dopamine is synthesised and released by other retinal cells, and does not replace glutamate at rod synapses.

questions.stem: Blocking transducin activation while leaving retinal photoisomerisation intact would chiefly prevent what?
questions.why: The photon can still change retinal configuration, but activated transducin is needed to relay this change to PDE6. Blocking transducin therefore prevents the normal rapid increase in cGMP breakdown.

notes.A: The direct photochemical isomerisation of retinal is intact under the stated assumption.
notes.B: The Schiff base forms between retinal and opsin within the pigment before the signal reaches transducin.
notes.D: Opsin synthesis occurs through gene expression and does not depend on acute activation of transducin.
notes.E: Photon absorption occurs in the visual pigment and lies upstream of transducin activation.

questions.stem: Which enzyme begins the shut-off of light-activated rhodopsin by phosphorylating it?
questions.why: Rhodopsin kinase, also called GRK1, phosphorylates active rhodopsin. This allows arrestin to bind and suppress further activation of transducin.

notes.A: Ribonucleotide reductase supplies precursors for DNA synthesis and does not phosphorylate visual pigment.
notes.B: PDE6 hydrolyses cGMP during signalling rather than modifying the activated receptor.
notes.C: Carbonic anhydrase interconverts carbon dioxide and bicarbonate and does not act as a pigment kinase.
notes.D: Adenylate kinase interconverts adenine nucleotides and does not transfer phosphate to rhodopsin.

questions.stem: What is the function of arrestin binding phosphorylated rhodopsin?
questions.why: Arrestin binds phosphorylated active rhodopsin and blocks productive interaction with transducin. This stops the receptor from activating additional G proteins after a flash.

notes.A: Arrestin decreases further transducin activation by occupying the phosphorylated receptor.
notes.C: The enzyme that hydrolyses cGMP is PDE6 rather than arrestin.
notes.D: Retinal regeneration requires the visual cycle and is not catalysed by arrestin.
notes.E: Channel opening requires cGMP binding. Arrestin influences this indirectly by shutting off the receptor.

questions.stem: What is the intrinsic transducin reaction that helps terminate the light signal?
questions.why: Transducin alpha has intrinsic GTPase activity. Conversion of bound GTP to GDP inactivates the alpha subunit, allowing PDE6 activity to return towards baseline.

notes.A: Transducin alpha switches off by hydrolysing a guanine nucleotide rather than ATP.
notes.B: Transducin's substrate is its bound GTP rather than an adenine nucleotide.
notes.C: Retinal reduction to retinol belongs to retinoid metabolism and is distinct from G-protein inactivation.
notes.E: Guanylate cyclase makes cGMP from GTP during recovery, while transducin itself hydrolyses its own GTP.

questions.stem: Which enzyme restores cGMP levels so that dark-current channels can reopen?
questions.why: Retinal guanylate cyclase converts GTP to cGMP during response recovery. Rising cGMP allows outer-segment cation channels to open again.

notes.B: PDE6 breaks down cGMP and therefore acts in the opposite direction to the recovery reaction.
notes.C: Rhodopsin kinase helps shut down receptor signalling and does not directly replenish cGMP.
notes.D: Retinal dehydrogenases act on vitamin A derivatives and do not synthesise cyclic nucleotides.
notes.E: ATP synthase makes ATP using a proton gradient. Recovery of the dark current requires cGMP instead.

questions.stem: Why does the calcium concentration inside illuminated rod outer segments fall?

options.label: A
options.text: Calcium export stops while entry continues

options.label: B
options.text: Calcium is consumed to generate cGMP

options.label: C
options.text: Calcium entry falls while extrusion continues

options.label: D
options.text: Calcium becomes bound permanently to opsin

options.label: E
options.text: Calcium is converted enzymatically to sodium

questions.why: Closure of the cGMP-gated channels blocks influx while the exchanger continues calcium extrusion.

notes.A: Calcium extrusion continues during the light response, while closure of the channels reduces entry.
notes.B: Guanylate cyclase uses GTP to make cGMP. Calcium can regulate this process without being consumed.
notes.D: Calcium concentration declines because of an imbalance between entry and extrusion, rather than permanent binding to opsin.
notes.E: Calcium and sodium remain distinct elements. Their gradients are coupled by an ion exchanger.

questions.stem: How does falling cytosolic calcium assist recovery after a light response?

options.label: B
options.text: It locks transducin in its active state

options.label: D
options.text: It blocks all guanylate cyclase activity

questions.why: Low calcium causes guanylate cyclase-activating proteins to stimulate retinal guanylate cyclase. Faster cGMP production helps reopen cyclic nucleotide-gated channels and recover sensitivity.

notes.A: PDE hydrolysis lowers cGMP, whereas the calcium feedback described here helps replace it.
notes.B: Transducin inactivation depends on hydrolysis of bound GTP and is not blocked by the recovery-associated fall in calcium.
notes.C: A dedicated kinase phosphorylates rhodopsin. Calcium cannot directly transfer phosphate to it.
notes.D: Lower calcium increases guanylate cyclase activity through calcium-sensitive regulatory proteins.

questions.stem: Which ion transport mechanism normally extrudes calcium from rod outer segments?
questions.why: The outer-segment sodium–calcium–potassium exchanger uses inward sodium movement to drive extrusion of calcium together with potassium. It continues exporting calcium when light reduces cation entry.

notes.A: Sodium–glucose cotransport moves glucose across certain epithelia and is not the normal rod calcium efflux mechanism.
notes.C: The outer-segment exchanger is driven by ion gradients and does not exchange calcium for ATP-driven chloride transport.
notes.D: Proton-linked phosphate uptake does not remove calcium through the rod's specific exchanger.
notes.E: Potassium–chloride cotransport handles those two ions and has no directly coupled calcium flux.

questions.stem: Why is dark adaptation delayed when visual-pigment regeneration is impaired?

options.label: A
options.text: All cones must regenerate into rods

options.label: E
options.text: Synaptic glutamate stores are permanently lost

questions.why: Recovery of rod sensitivity depends in part on regeneration of bleached rhodopsin. If the supply of 11-cis-retinal is slowed, fewer rod pigments are ready to detect weak illumination.

notes.A: Rods and cones remain distinct photoreceptors. Dark adaptation changes sensitivity without changing one class into the other.
notes.B: The response depends on recovery of pigment in existing cells and does not require retinal cell division.
notes.C: Rhodopsin regeneration takes place in retinal photoreceptors with support from the visual cycle, not in the lens.
notes.E: Changes in synaptic transmission are reversible and do not require permanent loss of glutamate storage.

questions.stem: What produces different spectral sensitivities among the three classes of cone pigment?
questions.why: Cones use the same 11-cis-retinal chromophore but different opsins tune their wavelength sensitivity.

notes.B: The different cone pigments generally use the same 11-cis-retinal chromophore, so the tuning comes from their proteins.
notes.C: Calcium regulates aspects of photoreceptor signalling but its chemical identity does not vary among cone classes.
notes.D: Cone spectral tuning reflects interactions with different opsins rather than distinct carbon isotopes in retinal.
notes.E: Retinal is a retinoid aldehyde and does not contain ribose phosphate groups.

questions.stem: Which approximate wavelength corresponds to the lecture's blue cone absorption maximum?
questions.why: The lecture lists approximate blue, green and red cone maxima at 455, 530 and 625 nm.

questions.stem: A person lacks a working green-sensitive cone pigment. Which molecular defect is most likely?
questions.why: Green-sensitive M cones use a distinct medium-wavelength opsin. Loss or spectral alteration of this opsin can compromise discrimination of red and green wavelengths.

notes.A: Rhodopsin is the rod pigment and its disruption primarily affects scotopic vision.
notes.B: The green-sensitive pigment requires an opsin expressed in retinal cones rather than platelet proteins.
notes.C: Loss of myelin could affect neural transmission but does not selectively remove the M-cone pigment.
notes.D: Guanylate cyclase participates downstream in phototransduction and does not determine the spectrum of green-sensitive opsin.

questions.stem: Why are common red-green colour vision disorders more frequent in males?

options.label: A
options.text: All relevant cone opsin genes are Y-linked

options.label: B
options.text: Many cone opsin genes are X-linked

options.label: D
options.text: The trait requires paternal mitochondrial DNA

options.label: E
options.text: All cone signals depend on testosterone

questions.why: The red and green cone opsin genes lie on the X chromosome, making recessive defects more evident in males.

notes.A: The common red–green defects are linked to genes on the X chromosome rather than the Y chromosome.
notes.C: The common inherited forms involve nuclear opsin genes rather than mitochondrial DNA.
notes.D: The common inherited forms arise from nuclear opsin genes rather than mitochondrial DNA.
notes.E: Cone signalling does not require a male-specific hormone; the sex difference follows from X-linked inheritance.
